title: Felix and the Well
premise: Hospice nurse Jonah Okonkwo has spent his life keeping quiet, counting doors, and listening to the dying count backwards toward something no one names. When he takes a live-in position with the Hartwell family caring for their matriarch, the house's mirrors begin reflecting a second behind reality—and in that lag, Jonah sees the family's futures being counted down alongside the dying woman. As the lag stretches and the well beneath the house begins to answer, Jonah must choose between the anonymity he's built his survival on and the love he never planned to feel for the Hartwells. He gets them out ahead of the final count by taking the old woman's place in it, discovering that belonging was never about staying invisible—it ends with the well closing, Jonah's name finally spoken aloud by the family who remembers him.
about_author: N. M. Hartwell is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who writes horror drawn from the hush of hospital corridors and the things patients say at 3 a.m. They live in a drafty house with too many mirrors and one very old well, which they insist is fine.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At the hospice, Mrs. Adeyemi counts backwards from thirty as she dies, and Jonah writes the number down—again. Establishes his rituals: lights on, doors counted, himself unseen. Emotional beat: weary competence masking loneliness; the reader senses he's counting something of his own.

chapters.title: Live-In Position
chapters.summary: Jonah accepts a private post at the Hartwell house: care for matriarch Edith, terminal but lucid. The house is beautiful, old, and built around a capped stone well in the back garden. Emotional beat: cautious hope—he wants to belong somewhere without being seen.

chapters.title: The Hartwells
chapters.summary: Jonah meets the family: pragmatic son Marcus, brittle daughter-in-law Claire, sharp-witted teen granddaughter Wren, and Edith herself, who looks at Jonah like she's counting him. Emotional beat: the ache of being an outsider at a family's most intimate hour.

chapters.title: Edith's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. She counts backwards in her sleep, but her numbers don't descend—they skip. She tells Jonah the house taught her to count. Emotional beat: dread braided with tenderness; Edith knows more than she says.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the hallway mirror, his raised hand lags a heartbeat behind his body. He tests every mirror in the house; all reflect one second late. Emotional beat: cold vertigo—the first crack in his controlled world.

chapters.title: Doors and Numbers
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren, who counts compulsively too, notices Jonah's rituals and quietly mirrors them. She tells him the mirrors started lagging the week Edith stopped sleeping. Emotional beat: two counters recognizing each other; first bond.

chapters.title: What the Lag Shows
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the lagged reflection, Jonah sees the room as it will be one second from now—then, worse, as it was. In the hallway mirror he glimpses a woman in Edith's nightgown standing where Edith isn't. Emotional beat: dread deepening into certainty.

chapters.title: The Well Cap
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus remembers childhood warnings never to sit on the well cap. He finds the iron seal scratched from beneath—long scratches, patient ones. Emotional beat: a son's denial cracking; he hides the evidence from the family.

chapters.title: Night Rounds
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At 3 a.m. Jonah hears Edith counting—backwards, from a number too large for a human life. The house's lights flicker in rhythm with her voice. Emotional beat: the nurse's instinct to comfort colliding with the instinct to run.

chapters.title: Claire's Reflection
chapters.summary: Claire's POV. Claire, exhausted and resentful, sees her own reflection smile when she doesn't. She tells no one, certain she's unraveling. Emotional beat: isolation; the house preys on whoever is most alone in a full house.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession
chapters.summary: Edith's POV, lucid at dawn. Edith admits she was born in this house, that her twin drowned in the well at seven, and that the family has been 'paying the count' ever since—someone always dies on schedule. Emotional beat: guilt passed down like an heirloom.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah finds Edith's hidden ledger: dates, names, and descending numbers spanning a century of Hartwell deaths—each entry ending in zero. The next line is blank except for a date three weeks away. Emotional beat: horror becoming arithmetic.

chapters.title: Marcus Refuses
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Jonah shows Marcus the ledger. Marcus burns it, calling it a dying woman's nonsense—but he can't burn the memory of the scratches. Emotional beat: love expressed as denial; the family's fault lines widen.

chapters.title: Wren's Experiment
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren films the mirror and times the lag: exactly one second, but the lag is growing—1.2 seconds now. In the footage's final frame, something in the reflected hallway turns to face the camera. Emotional beat: teenage bravado curdling into real fear.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah hears a second voice counting under Edith's—a child's voice, hoarse from water. It counts in Jonah's own rhythm, the way he counts doors. Emotional beat: the house has learned him; his rituals have become a handle it can grip.

chapters.title: Leaving Is Counted Too
chapters.summary: Claire's POV. Claire tries to leave with Wren; the car dies at the gate, and every clock in the house reads the same wrong minute. They walk back inside to find the front door standing open onto the hallway—both doors. Emotional beat: claustrophobia; the house is polite about keeping them.

chapters.title: What Jonah Was Running From
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, flashback. Jonah's own family died in a fire he survived by counting exits instead of saving them. He has been invisible ever since, believing attention is what gets people killed. Emotional beat: the theme surfaces—his invisibility was never safety, just a slower grief.

chapters.title: Edith Stops Counting
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith refuses to count anymore, and the house retaliates: the mirrors show the family's futures running backwards, unwinding. Wren's reflection begins to fade. Emotional beat: a matriarch's sacrifice instinct; the count needs a voice.

chapters.title: The Well Opens Its Mouth
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. The well cap sits ajar, the iron seal folded open like a page. Cold air rises, and with it the smell of the pond where Edith's twin drowned. Emotional beat: the past is not past; Marcus finally believes and is ashamed it took this long.

chapters.title: Family Meeting
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah lays out everything—the ledger's logic, the lag, the date. For the first time, he speaks as one of them, and the family listens. Emotional beat: the invisible man becomes visible; belonging begins with being believed.

chapters.title: The Twin's Name
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith finally speaks her twin's name—Adaeze—which no one has said aloud in seventy years. The whole house exhales; every mirror shows the hallway empty for the first time. Emotional beat: naming as both wound and key.

chapters.title: Adaeze
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV, the drowned twin. A chapter from below: patient, waterlogged, not evil but owed. She has been counting the family down because no one ever counted her. Emotional beat: pity inside terror; the monster has a grievance.

chapters.title: Bargaining at the Cap
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah goes to the well and bargains: take his count, not theirs. The child's voice laughs and names his price—not his death, but his name, his face, his being-remembered. Emotional beat: the bargain strikes at exactly what Jonah fears and what he's begun to want.

chapters.title: The Lag Reaches Ten
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The mirror lag hits ten seconds; the reflections now show the family living days the family hasn't lived yet—Claire laughing, Marcus packing, Wren grown. The house is showing them the futures it will keep if they pay. Emotional beat: temptation dressed as prophecy.

chapters.title: Claire Breaks
chapters.summary: Claire's POV. Claire, shown a reflection of a life without Edith's care and Wren's fear, almost says yes to the house. Jonah talks her back from the mirror by holding her hand where the reflection can't reach. Emotional beat: love against the house's counterfeit love.

chapters.title: Marcus Digs
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus excavates around the well and finds the twin's small bones were never recovered—only her shoes, kept in Edith's trunk, and a funeral that never happened. Emotional beat: the family's debt is a ceremony undone; grief with nowhere to go.

chapters.title: The Empty Bed
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Edith dies quietly on schedule—the count's date arriving early because she stopped counting. The house dims, satisfied, and the mirrors go still. Jonah realizes the count didn't end; it transferred. Emotional beat: hollow grief; they paid without meaning to.

chapters.title: The New Number
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finds the ledger's blank line filled in her own handwriting she never wrote: her name, and a number descending. The house has chosen its next voice. Emotional beat: terror of inheritance; the count wants the young.

chapters.title: Jonah's Choice
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah understands the transfer: the count follows whoever the house can see most clearly, and Wren has become visible. He decides to make himself the loudest thing in the house—deliberately, for the first time. Emotional beat: the theme crystallizes; invisibility abandoned as strategy.

chapters.title: Rituals Reversed
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah breaks every ritual: lights off, doors uncounted, and he speaks his own full name aloud to the empty hallway. The mirrors all turn, so to speak, toward him. Emotional beat: self-erasure inverted into self-offering; fear and resolve in equal measure.

chapters.title: Wren Fights Too
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren refuses to be saved quietly; she and Jonah argue—she won't let him vanish for her, because vanishing is what he's always done. Emotional beat: love as friction; she demands he survive the story too.

chapters.title: The Funeral That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Claire's POV. The family holds Adaeze's funeral at the well: her name spoken, her shoes buried, Edith's seventy-year-old apology read aloud. The mirrors lag backwards—showing the past settling. Emotional beat: the family pays its true debt; the house grows quiet, almost kind.

chapters.title: But the Count Remains
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The funeral settles Adaeze, but the count itself—a older, hungrier arithmetic beneath her—remains, and it has accepted Jonah's offer. The date on the ledger is now tonight. Emotional beat: the calm before; the family spends its last hours together honestly.

chapters.title: Last Supper
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, rotating paragraphs. The Hartwells and Jonah share a final dinner: laughter, Wren's terrible jokes, Claire's good wine, Marcus saying thank you. Emotional beat: the belonging Jonah fled from his whole life, given to him on his last night.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At midnight Jonah walks to the well, and the house opens the way for him—every door leading to the garden. The child-voice and something older count him down from ten. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into purpose; he counts with them instead of against them.

chapters.title: The Zero
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, at the bottom. In the well, Jonah meets the count itself—an old hunger that has eaten every Hartwell generation's endings. He offers it his name, his face, his remembrance, and it takes them—and in taking them, it becomes finite, nameable, and ends. Emotional beat: sacrifice as authorship; he gives the story its last word.

chapters.title: The House Goes Quiet
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The mirrors show only the present, exactly on time. The well cap seals itself with a sound like a book closing. But no one can remember the nurse's face—only that someone was loved here. Emotional beat: victory with a wound in it.

chapters.title: The Empty Room
chapters.summary: Claire's POV. The family finds Jonah's room: his notebooks of counts, and on the last page, not numbers but the family's names, each one written carefully, as if memorizing them was the point. Emotional beat: grief and gratitude; the invisible man's only legacy is them.

chapters.title: Counting Forward
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren begins a new ledger: names and dates of living, counting up instead of down. The family keeps Jonah's rituals transformed—lights on, doors counted, and now, always, one extra place at the table. Emotional beat: mourning turned into practice; love against duty resolved into love as duty.

chapters.title: One Second On Time
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, coda—somewhere adjacent. A mirror, somewhere, reflects a man a second early instead of late, walking toward a door that opens for him. He is not remembered, but he is not gone; the count goes forward now, and it carries his name where no one can hear it. Emotional beat: quiet, uncanny peace—the horror's residue and the love's reward in the same breath.
